note: Attacker-controlled bytes become the source buffer for all later parsing paths.
The first two input bytes choose the allocated buffer length for the ASN.1 parser.
A heap buffer of attacker-selected size is allocated and then filled from the remaining input.
One input byte selects the execution path; the crash-relevant path is the ASN.1 validation branch.
The chosen heap buffer is handed to the recursive ASN.1 validator as untrusted input.
Validation begins by recursively decoding the attacker-controlled buffer from offset 0.
The first byte is interpreted as ASN.1 type metadata, including the constructed bit and tag number.
A high-tag-number form triggers a loop that keeps reading continuation bytes from the same buffer.

code: while (byte_index < bytes_max && long_type <= type_number_limit) { next_byte = bytes[byte_index++]; ... }
note: The loop advances byte_index while consuming continuation bytes; malformed or truncated encodings can leave the parser near the end of the buffer.

code: ptls_asn1_read_length(bytes, bytes_max, byte_index, &length, &indefinite_length, &last_byte, decode_error, level, log_ctx);
note: The next byte sequence is decoded as a length field, which determines the recursive bounds for child elements.
The vulnerable path is reached when the parser is driven into edge-case length encodings near the end of the buffer.
The recursive descent uses byte_index and last_byte as bounds, but the loop condition still permits a read of bytes[byte_index] at the current frontier.
When the malformed ASN.1 structure drives recursion to the boundary, this direct byte read can step past the allocated heap object, causing the ASAN heap-buffer-overflow read.
